Symptoms are mainly upper-airway: nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, with some patients having mild cough or mild fever; most recover in 5–7 days. The virus replicates best at 33–35°C in the nasal cavity; at 37°C in the lungs, activity is inhibited, so lower-airway disease is uncommon. Management is supportive: rest, fluids, humidified air, saline nasal irrigation, and infection control. articleHeadline: Anak Lahir Musim Panas Dinilai Lebih Rentan Terkena Flu
articleSummary: As of 30 June 2026, Harian Jogja (Yogyakarta, Indonesia) reports that babies born in summer have a higher risk of influenza infection than those born in autumn or winter. The difference stems from routine pediatric check-ups and influenza vaccine timing, not genetics or climate. Citing Parents, the study notes many health systems schedule visits by birth month; summer-born children often have check-ups before school starts when vaccines are not yet widely available. Autumn- or winter-born children typically receive vaccines when shots are readily accessible, enabling vaccination in a single visit. The resulting administrative gap can leave summer-born children under-protected ahead of flu season, with potential complications such as ear infections, pneumonia, or hospitalization. Experts urge reminders and more flexible scheduling to ensure equitable vaccination, including in Indonesia.

articleSummary: Terminal ileitis is inflammation of the terminal ileum, the last part of the small intestine. While commonly linked to Crohn's disease, it is not exclusive to Crohn's and can follow infections (Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter), tuberculosis (notably relevant in India), prolonged NSAID use, reduced blood flow, autoimmune or vascular disorders, or a temporary inflammatory process. The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile acids, so inflammation can impair nutrient absorption and cause digestive problems and nutritional deficiencies. Terminal ileitis is a red flag rather than a disease. Symptoms include lower right abdominal pain, chronic or recurrent diarrhea, fatigue, low-grade fever, and sometimes blood in stool. In Crohn's, ulcers, bleeding, strictures, and fistulas may occur. If untreated, there is a risk of obstruction and spread of infection with higher hospitalization; early diagnosis and cause-specific treatment are essential.

articleHeadline: Climate variability and COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions shaped dengue transmission in Guangdong: an integrated modeling study
articleSummary: Dengue fever in Guangdong, China was shaped by climate variability and COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). An integrated modeling framework combines climate-driven mosquito abundance estimated by recurrent neural networks with a temperature- and intervention-sensitive SIR model, calibrated on 2016–2023 data (mosquito surveillance, meteorology, NPI intensity, and reported dengue cases) within a partially observed Markov process. The model reproduces interannual dengue fluctuations using shared parameters. SHAP analysis shows nonlinear day–night temperature effects, with minimum temperature emerging as a relatively influential climatic driver, while temperature-dependent biting rates critically determine transmission. COVID-19 NPIs substantially suppressed dengue incidence in Guangdong during the pandemic, estimated at 99.03% reduction (95% CI 94.54–99.68%) versus a weak-intervention counterfactual. The framework disentangles mosquito abundance, temperature-driven biting, and human interventions, offering a climate-informed tool for early warning and intervention assessment for dengue and other climate-sensitive vector-borne diseases.

articleSummary: As of June 30, 2026, Oropouche virus may have infected 9.4 million people in Latin America and the Caribbean since 1960, with Brazil alone around 5.5 million infections. Manaus, in the Amazon, is a hotspot, estimated 300,000 infections—260 times higher than official counts. The outbreaks trace to two waves in the 1980s and in the recent surge, each exposing more than 12% of the population. The illness causes acute dengue-like symptoms—fever, headache, myalgia, and joint pains—but can progress to severe complications, including encephalitis and liver problems, and may include miscarriages or fetal abnormalities. Researchers note that about 1 in 1,000 infections may evolve into serious neurological disorders. Transmission occurs via Gunpowder Midge, a tiny insect not reliant on mosquitoes, thriving in moist soil in forests and farms; urban spraying may be ineffective. Antibodies from older strains partly neutralize the newer one, per studies in Nature Medicine and Nature Medicine Health.

articleSummary: DNA from an Ehrlichia-related genotype was detected in 7.69% (2/26) of sampled free-ranging anteaters in southeastern Brazil, and an Anaplasma genotype in 3.85% (1/26). articleHeadline: Why fungal infections rise during the Kolkata monsoon, and what you can do to stay safe
articleSummary: Kolkata’s monsoon drives a surge in fungal infections as humidity and prolonged moisture foster fungi on skin. Commonly affected areas include the feet, groin, underarms and skin folds, with itching, redness, rashes and irritation. Risk factors include damp clothing, wet shoes, sweating, poor drying after bathing, tight non-breathable garments, and, for some, weak immunity or diabetes. Frequent infections are athlete’s foot, ringworm, scalp and nail infections, and jock itch; fungi that affect the lungs—aspergillosis, cryptococcosis and blastomycosis—can be life-threatening for the immunocompromised if neglected. Preventive measures: stay dry, change wet clothes and shoes promptly, wear loose cotton garments, dry between toes and skin folds, and ensure footwear is completely dry; avoid sharing towels, socks or footwear. Leptospirosis risk rises from floodwater; avoid barefoot exposure, cover wounds, and maintain sanitation and rodent control. Seek medical care if symptoms persist or spread.

articleHeadline: Clinical characteristics, management, and visual outcomes of presumed infectious and non-infectious anterior scleritis in a tuberculosis-endemic Indonesian Tertiary Center - International Ophthalmology
articleSummary: 69 patients (96 eyes) with presumed infectious and non-infectious anterior scleritis were studied at Indonesia’s tertiary Dr. Cipto Mangunkusumo National General Hospital from 2019–2023. Mean age 38.5 years; majority female. Non-infectious scleritis accounted for 56 eyes (58.3%), presumed infectious for 40 eyes (41.7%). Presumed infectious disease was mainly tuberculosis-associated; non-infectious etiologies included idiopathic disease and spondyloarthropathy. Nodular scleritis predominated in the presumed infectious group, while diffuse scleritis was more frequent in the non-infectious group. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was the most common systemic treatment in presumed infectious scleritis; non-infectious cases were managed with NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and steroid-sparing agents. Conclusion: in tuberculosis-endemic settings, careful etiologic evaluation, close follow-up, and multidisciplinary management are warranted; limitations include retrospective design, incomplete follow-up, and limited microbiologic confirmation.

articleHeadline: IIT-Kharagpur develops 'CliMed' framework for dengue risk assessment
articleSummary: India's IIT Kharagpur has developed CliMed, a climate-informed, spatially explicit framework for dengue risk assessment across India. The model fuses daily climate data, land use, population, settlement context and Aedes mosquito-species suitability to generate interpretable risk signals for dengue transmission. Focusing on Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, CliMed reads interacting drivers; temperature affects biting and virus incubation; rainfall creates or disrupts breeding; humidity influences mosquito activity; land-use and population distribution shape human exposure. It provides multiple indicators beyond reported cases, including a count-oriented output mapping where newly exposed people may concentrate, helping distinguish ecological transmission pressure from burden. Designed for national, state, district, campus or custom areas with suitable gridded inputs, CliMed supports preparedness and vector-control planning by complementing institutional case data with environmental and vector-driven risk assessments.

A UNDP socio-economic assessment warns the crisis could push nearly 1 million more people into poverty and cost Africa billions, with Uganda, Rwanda and South Sudan also affected. Containment and border restrictions disrupt local economies and livelihoods. The report estimates a decline of over $1 billion in the DRC and 55,000 jobs lost there; cross-border trade disruptions could shave $2.37 billion from Africa’s GDP. Poor households could see daily consumption fall by 1.76%. The crisis is gendered: women in cross-border trade and frontline health workers bear the heaviest burden. Health resource diversion could cause up to 2,520 under-5 deaths in the DRC for non-Ebola causes. Recommendations include a multi-layer framework with cash transfers, border screening, emergency funding for maternal and child health, and investments in health systems, social protection and resilience.

articleHeadline: Больные в Болгарию завозят различные заболевания
articleSummary: Imported diseases increasingly reach Bulgaria as patients return from abroad. Bulgarian patients bring dengue fever and chikungunya into Bulgaria, with no local transmission detected yet, but rising imported cases. Aedes albopictus, now widespread across Europe including Bulgaria, can act as a vector for these tropical viruses. Dengue is most often reported among tourists returning from the Maldives; chikungunya is imported from the Seychelles. Confirmations occur at Bulgaria's National Center for Infectious and Parasitic Diseases, the sole facility able to verify such diagnoses. Preventive measures for travelers include repellents and clothing coverage. Separately, Vibrio vulnificus, a seawater bacterium that infects via skin wounds, poses risks in warm months; rare on the Bulgarian Black Sea coast but common in Thailand, Japan, Korea, the US, and Canada. Infections can progress rapidly in those with chronic disease, requiring urgent care.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in Bunia, DR Congo, has no licensed vaccine or therapy, prompting Africa CDC to seek $16 million within days to close a $18 million therapeutics-trials funding gap for the Bundibugyo strain. articleSummary: IIIT Kharagpur researchers propose CliMed (Climate-informed and Spatially Explicit Modelling Framework) to forecast dengue fever spread across India by integrating climate, geography, and social factors. The model analyzes two key Aedes vectors, Aedes aegypti in urban areas and Aedes albopictus in peri-urban zones, to map seasonal risk. It uses daily temperature, rainfall, and humidity, plus housing density and land use, to assess how vector biology and virus transmission respond to conditions. Output includes population-based risk and climate-vector pressure indicators to guide preemptive interventions, addressing underreporting delays in hospital data. The system aims to provide early warning at national, state, district, or large campus levels, enabling health authorities to target resources and control measures before outbreaks emerge. articleSummary: As of 2026-06-30, Toxoplasma gondii, a common parasite carried by cats, could infect up to a third of the world’s population and trigger serious ocular disease. Most infections are asymptomatic, but immune-compromised individuals may have flu-like symptoms; ocular infection causes eye pain, redness, blurred vision, and floaters, with severe cases risking retinal inflammation and permanent blindness. The study, published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases, is led by João Furtado (University of São Paulo) and Justine Smith (Flinders University), uniting experts from the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia. Transmission occurs via undercooked meat, contaminated water or produce, and cat feces; improved food safety, water, sanitation and antenatal care could reduce impacts. articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola in the DRC: a crisis that threatens to worsen poverty.
articleHeadline: Ebola en RDC : une crise qui menace d'aggraver la pauvreté
articleSummary: As of June 30, 2026, the Ebola outbreak in the DRC, caused by Bundibugyo virus (no vaccine or treatment), has 1,274 cases and 360 deaths, with the epicenter in Ituri (1,165 cases, 301 deaths). The outbreak has spread to Haut-Uélé, adding to previous provinces Ituri, Nord-Kivu, and Sud-Kivu. Declared May 15, the crisis poses a sweeping poverty and economic shock: the DRC could incur over $1 billion in real GDP losses and about 55,000 job losses; Africa-wide GDP could drop by $2.37 billion due to trade disruptions and border controls. The most vulnerable, notably women-led households and female traders, bear the brunt. Indirect health impacts may add up to 2,520 infant deaths from non-Ebola causes. The PNUD urges targeted cash transfers, tailored border measures, and protection of maternal/child health services, along with sustained investment in health systems and social protection.

articleHeadline: Ebola epidemic: WHO says Congo outbreak spreading faster than response capabilities
articleSummary: The World Health Organization warns that the Bundibugyo virus disease Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is spreading faster than response capacity. By June 28, 2026, there were 1,307 confirmed cases and 377 deaths (case fatality 28.8%), with 259 new cases in the week of June 21–28. The outbreak is expanding to 35 health zones, with Ituri Province (Mandima Health Zone) accounting for about 90% of recent cases; Bunia, Rwampara and Mongbwalu are major hotspots. Treatment capacity is strained: 654 beds nationwide with 96.2% occupancy, and North Kivu centers at 138.8% occupancy. Contact tracing remains a critical gap: 9,968 identified contacts, 81.3% reached in the last 24 hours. Responders have expanded labs, surveillance and border controls; about 116 billion Kenyan Shillings has been pledged, to be rapidly converted into operational support. An imported Bundibugyo case in France from Ituri underscores ongoing international export risk; Uganda remains vulnerable due to cross-border movement.

articleHeadline: Ebola Outbreak Could Cost Africa Up to $3.6bn, UN Warns
articleSummary: Ebola virus disease (Bundibugyo strain) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda. By 28 June, DRC has 1,307 infections and 377 deaths since declaration on 15 May; Uganda reports 20 cases and two deaths, with most linked to travel from DRC and some local transmission. Neighboring South Sudan and other countries face regional risk. Economic impact could reach up to $3.6 billion and 328,000 lost jobs if transmission spreads regionally; best-case Congo GDP loss around $1 billion. No licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo; WHO notes candidates are being tested. Transmission occurs via contact with infected bodily fluids, contaminated materials, and during burials. Affected DR Congo provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu. Response hampered by conflict; risk levels: DR Congo very high, Uganda high. WHO discourages travel restrictions; emphasis on community trust and safe burials; funding needs include $518m health spending and $1.4bn with humanitarian needs; DR Congo government has a $319m plan.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Volunteers risk their lives to halt Ebola. They are not always welcome.
articleHeadline: Voluntários arriscam a vida para travar o ébola. Nem sempre são bem-vindos
articleSummary: As of 30 June 2026, Red Cross volunteers in Bunia, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, are pivotal in Ebola virus disease containment, performing safe burials deemed crucial to halting a transmission chain that experts fear could mark the region’s worst outbreak. Front-line workers face ongoing infection risk and hostility from terrified communities. Ramazani Bokwandela, 61, a Red Cross volunteer who once sold gasoline, describes improvising to stay on duty: tearing the sleeves from his Red Cross tunic, using a snail shell as a blade, and slipping into the bushes; then grabbing a bunch of plants to masquerade as a farmer. The report highlights the essential, perilous role of local responders in stopping Ebola spread amid fear and resistance in the Congo.

articleHeadline: Idosos sem vacina da gripe lideram casos graves por influenza no ES - Folha Vitória
articleSummary: Influenza remains a serious burden in Espírito Santo, Brazil, with 21 deaths from the severe form to date; 14 of these fatalities occurred among unvaccinated elderly individuals. Vaccination coverage for seniors is only 45.13% as of June 25, well below the 90% target; last year’s elderly coverage was 56.45%. Among children under 6, 46.02% are vaccinated, while 127 severe cases occurred in unvaccinated people, including 41 in children aged 6 months to under 6 years; pediatric coverage last year was 74.35% of a 90% goal. Vaccines are updated annually, and protection begins about two weeks after vaccination. The immunization effort emphasizes preventing hospitalizations and deaths even during peak circulation. Flu shots are available in 700+ vaccination sites across Espírito Santo, available to all from six months old; routine vaccination for elderly, pregnant women, and children 6 months to under 6 years remains key.

articleHeadline: Rio Grande do Sul implementa seguro total para rebanho bovino contra febre aftosa
articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) insurance coverage expands in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, to protect nearly 11 million cattle (beef and dairy) with a 12‑month APSE policy totaling R$50 million. The program, unique among Brazilian states, guarantees indemnities to producers for losses linked to FMD and is funded by Fundesa, with a deductible of up to R$13 million and a per‑animal premium of about R$0.18. The move reinforces sanitary safeguards for a herd largely composed of European breeds, preserving genetics and production continuity. Vigilance remains necessary as the virus is not eradicated globally, with recent cases in Asia and Europe.

articleHeadline: Ebola crosses into Europe as WHO warns international spread risk remains high

Uganda reports 21 linked cases via the DRC–Uganda corridor, including a truck driver who fell ill before crossing into Kampala. WHO urges stronger traveller surveillance, cross-border coordination, postponement of large gatherings, and international support.

articleHeadline: Giant African snails enter school campuses in Tirunavaya, raising health concerns for children
articleSummary: Giant African snail (Lissachatina fulica) infestation spreads to Tirunavaya panchayat in Kerala, India, entering school campuses with snails observed on playgrounds, walls, and classrooms, risking children and teachers. Preventive measures include blocking entry points with mesh screens and wearing gloves when handling snails; some residents use salt or tobacco-copper sulphate to kill them. articleSummary: Brazilian spotted fever is a bacterial infection caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by the star tick. Although relatively rare, it is a severe disease with reemerged in several regions of Brazil. Person-to-person transmission does not occur; infection happens only by bite of an infected tick, which releases bacteria into the host's bloodstream. The star tick is found in rural areas, forests, and zones near wild or domestic animals such as horses, cattle, and capybaras. Risk increases the longer the tick remains attached, especially beyond four hours. Symptoms typically appear 2-14 days after the bite and can resemble dengue or leptospirosis. Without rapid treatment, the disease can progress to renal, pulmonary, or neurological failure. Diagnosis is clinical, with exposure history; treatment is doxycycline, most effective when started early. Prevention focuses on environmental and animal control to reduce tick presence.

articleSummary: Mpox (monkeypox) surged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, triggering the World Health Organization’s highest international alert. Mpox has long circulated in the country, but emergent, more concerning forms amid health-system fragility and eastern conflict-driven displacement turned a local problem into a world-spanning emergency. The article frames this as a manifestation of global health inequality: vaccines, treatments, and funding arrive late and unevenly, while Congo bears the onus of protecting itself and others. Yet the country also wields real strengths: epidemiological experience, trained response structures, and resilient community networks. Beyond mpox, Congo grapples with malaria, measles, cholera, and malnutrition, reflecting a chronically under-resourced health system. The piece argues for building a strong, autonomous public health capacity to protect its people and deepen global health security. Appears in BETO’s Congo 66 series.

articleSummary: Fever-free malaria is spreading in West Bengal’s forested Western region (Jhargram, Bankura, Purulia) and North Bengal (Jalpaiguri, Alipurduar, Darjeeling’s Duars). In 2025, blood tests in forest belts detected asymptomatic malaria among tribal populations. During March–April this year, surveys and testing expanded; several individuals tested positive for Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium falciparum, triggering village-wide malaria-month screening. This is not a new species but a phenomenon of “forest malaria” in which longstanding immunity among local communities dampens symptoms. Health officials warn that asymptomatic carriers can silently sustain transmission, and if symptoms appear, the infection can be as severe as conventional malaria. The situation raises the risk of spread to tourists visiting these jungle areas.

articleHeadline: Relief Workers Say This Ebola Outbreak Could Take Six More Months to Bring Under Control
articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s eastern region, centered in Goma, has surpassed 1,100 confirmed cases as of late June 2026. Relief workers warn it could take six months or longer to bring under control. Dr. Abdou Sebushishe of International Medical Corps says contact tracing reaches only about 25% of contacts, and community distrust and reliance on traditional healers fuel transmission. WHO Africa Emergency Response Lead Dr. Rose Belizaire rates the current response at about 3–4 out of 10 and calls for a rapid scale-up of efforts. The response has expanded technically, with roughly 400 treatment beds and four operational laboratories, two capable of processing nearly 1,000 samples per day, but resources and personal protective equipment remain inadequate. Earlier counts fluctuated due to laboratory reclassification of suspected cases; by late June, confirmed cases exceed 1,100, indicating genuine outbreak growth. No approved Bundibugyo vaccine or treatment exists for this outbreak.
notes: 記事はコンゴ民主共和国東部（ゴマ、北キブ州）での大規模エボラ流行について報じている。確認症例1,100件超、6ヶ月以上の制御期間を要する予測、WHO評価3-4/10の低評点、接触者追跡の不十分性（25%）、ワクチンと承認治療法の不在など、複数の深刻な懸念要因を含む。フルRRA実施が必須。
